# Change-Set Grammar Reference

Complete reference for `glassfrog proposal grammar` — the read that tells you what
a proposal's `changes[]` array may say, before you assemble one.

## Overview

Building a proposal means assembling a `changes[]` array, and the knowledge of what
is sayable in it is split: the published Glassfrog API v5 contract carries the
change-type vocabulary and the nesting rule, while a handful of shapes the contract
does not describe are known only from observed server behavior. Neither half is
served at the point of assembly.

`glassfrog proposal grammar` serves both in one invocation.

```
glassfrog proposal grammar [--base-url URL] [-o FORMAT]
```

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| API operation | **none** — the command makes no request |
| Arguments | none (any positional is a usage error) |
| Command-local flags | none |
| Credentials | never resolved |
| Network | never contacted |
| Pagination | none — one invocation returns the whole reference |
| Exit codes | `0`, `2`, and `1` only (see [Error reference](#error-reference)) |

It is the only `glassfrog` command that produces output without talking to the API.
The knowledge is compiled into the binary, so the reference is available on any
machine that has the CLI — before `glassfrog auth login` has ever run, with no
credential configured, and with no connectivity. Output is identical online and
offline.

## The command informs; it never validates

This boundary is part of the contract, not a limitation to be worked around:

- **No argument or flag takes a change set.** A positional argument — including a
  path like `changes.json` — is refused as a usage error before any of the
  command's own code runs, and the refusal says nothing about the change set's
  validity, because nothing looked at it.
- The command **renders no verdict**. The server remains the only judge of whether
  a change set is valid. Reading the grammar reduces the chance of a refused
  round-trip; it does not replace one.
- Nothing tracks whether the reference was consulted. It has no state.

One thing not to misread: `-o stdin` reads piped text as **your output template**,
as it does on every read. Piping a change set to it is therefore not a check — the
document is rendered as a template (JSON with no `{{` renders as itself), so you get
your own file back and exit `0`. That zero means "the template rendered", never "the
change set is acceptable". There is no invocation that evaluates a change set.

A related trap the reference itself records: for one recorded shape the server
*accepts* the create and returns a `prp_` id, then reports the proposal invalid.
"Created" is not "valid" — see the `accepted-but-invalid` disposition below.

## What it renders

Two halves, each marked with where its knowledge comes from.

### The change-type vocabulary

Every change type the published contract enumerates, with the placement class that
says where the type may appear:

| Placement | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `top-level` | The part may sit directly in the `changes[]` array. |
| `nested-only` | The part must ride inside a wrapper part; it is refused as a top-level change. The entry names its wrappers. |

The nesting rule and its wrapper parts (`CreateRole`, `UpdateRole`) come from the
contract's own `ProposalChange` schema, so a contract refresh that changes them
changes what this command renders.

### The empirical residue

The shapes verified against live server behavior that the published contract does
not carry. Each entry states the shape to use, the disposition the server gives it,
and the symptom that getting the shape wrong produces.

| Disposition | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `accepted` | The server takes this shape. |
| `rejected` | The server refuses this shape. |
| `accepted-but-invalid` | The server accepts the create and returns a `prp_` id, but the proposal comes back invalid — a dead draft, not a successful governance change. |

These are verified observations that may change when the server changes, which is
exactly why they are marked differently from the contract-published half.

## Provenance

Every rendered shape carries its provenance, so a contract-published shape and a
verified observation are never confused. The two tokens are the complete set, and
agents compare them literally:

| Token | Applies to | Means |
|---|---|---|
| `published-contract` | every `change_types` entry | The published Glassfrog API v5 contract enumerates this. |
| `empirical-observation` | every `facts` entry | Observed server behavior, not part of the published contract. |

In `json`/`yaml` the token is a field on every entry. In `full`/`compact` the
contract-derived content and the empirical observations are rendered as separate,
visibly marked sections.

## Output formats

Format selection is the house chain, identical to every read: `-o`/`--output` flag
→ `GLASSFROG_OUTPUT` → the `output` key in the nearest `.glassfrogrc` → the
built-in default (`full`).

| Format | Output |
|---|---|
| `full` (default) | The vocabulary with each type's placement, the nesting rule stated once with its wrapper types, and every fact with its title, shape, disposition, and symptom — under provenance-marked section headings. |
| `compact` | The vocabulary condensed to one line per placement class, and each fact as one line carrying its id, disposition, and title. |
| `json` | The structured document below. |
| `yaml` | The same document in YAML. |
| a template file path | Your own `text/template`, applied over the same structure. |
| `stdin` | Your own template, read from a pipe. |

Both human formats state **"no empirical residue is currently recorded"** when the
residue is empty — the section never silently disappears, because a vanished
section makes a different claim from an empty one.

### Structured output

The document has exactly two keys, both always present:

| Key | Type | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `change_types` | array | one entry per change type the published contract enumerates |
| `facts` | array | one entry per recorded empirical fact; `[]` when the residue is empty — the key is never omitted |

`change_types[]` entry:

| Field | Type | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | string | the contract's enum member, verbatim (e.g. `CreatePolicy`) |
| `placement` | string | `top-level` \| `nested-only` |
| `wrappers` | array of strings | present **only** when `placement` is `nested-only` — the parts the type must ride inside |
| `provenance` | string | `published-contract` |

`facts[]` entry:

| Field | Type | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | string | the fact's permanent handle (`CSG-1`, `CSG-2`, …) — never reused |
| `title` | string | the fact's one-line heading |
| `shape` | string | the shape to use |
| `disposition` | string | `accepted` \| `rejected` \| `accepted-but-invalid` |
| `symptom` | string | the observable symptom of getting the shape wrong |
| `provenance` | string | `empirical-observation` |

Example (abbreviated — the real vocabulary carries every contract type):

```json
{
  "change_types": [
    {"type": "CreateAccountability", "placement": "nested-only", "wrappers": ["CreateRole", "UpdateRole"], "provenance": "published-contract"},
    {"type": "CreatePolicy", "placement": "top-level", "provenance": "published-contract"},
    {"type": "UpdateRole", "placement": "top-level", "provenance": "published-contract"}
  ],
  "facts": [
    {
      "id": "CSG-1",
      "title": "An own-circle policy is a top-level `CreatePolicy` part with no `UpdateRole` wrapper",
      "shape": "…",
      "disposition": "accepted",
      "symptom": "…",
      "provenance": "empirical-observation"
    }
  ]
}
```

**This document is not a `{data: …}` envelope.** Every other read's `json` output
reproduces the server's response envelope; this command has no response to mirror,
so `json` serializes the reference itself. That is a deliberate deviation, not an
oversight — the structure *is* the raw data.

### Determinism

The same binary always renders the same document: `change_types` is sorted
alphabetically by `type`, `facts` follow the record's own order, and `wrappers` is
sorted. Two invocations produce byte-identical structured output, so a consumer can
diff two runs or cache the result safely.

## Inherited flags

The leaf inherits the persistent root flags by cobra inheritance:

| Flag | Owner | Behavior here |
|---|---|---|
| `--base-url` | 011 | Parses and is **inert**. It is never resolved: a base URL only matters to a request, and this command makes none. |
| `-o`, `--output` | 020/035 | `full` (default) \| `compact` \| `json` \| `yaml` \| a template file path \| `stdin`. Participates fully. |

A user template (`-o <file>` or `-o stdin`) applies over the grammar structure
exactly as templates apply over read payloads. Template fields are the render
view's: `.ChangeTypes` (each `.Type`, `.Placement`), `.Groups` (the vocabulary
grouped by placement class), `.NestedOnly`, `.Wrappers`, and `.Facts` (each `.ID`,
`.Title`, `.Shape`, `.Disposition`, `.Symptom`), plus `.ContractProvenance` and
`.ObservedProvenance`. A missing or unparseable template source is a usage error
before anything renders.

The command defines no format flag of its own, and it takes no `--per-page`: there
is nothing to paginate.

## Error reference

| Condition | Outcome | Exit |
|---|---|---|
| Reference rendered | Success | 0 |
| Any positional argument — including a change set offered for checking | UsageError | 2 |
| Unknown flag | UsageError | 2 |
| Invalid `--output` value from the env or `.glassfrogrc`; missing, unreadable, or unparseable user template; `-o stdin` with no pipe | UsageError | 2 |
| Unreadable or unparseable `.glassfrogrc` | UsageError | 2 |
| The embedded reference fails to decode (a corrupt build) or a render fails | RuntimeError | 1 |

Usage errors follow every command's existing conduct: the cause and a help pointer
go to stderr, stdout stays empty, and no diagnostic ever includes the token.

**Exit codes 3–7 are unproducible by this command.** That is a contract fact, not
an aspiration: `APIError` (3), `PermissionError` (4), `RateLimited` (5),
`NetworkUnavailable` (6), and `StaleWrite` (7) all require a request, and no
request path exists here.

One clarification about the credential-free conduct: no *credential* is ever read,
so a garbage token cannot block this command. The credential is stored in
`.glassfrogrc`, which is also where the `output` setting lives — so a
`.glassfrogrc` that does not parse at all fails output resolution here exactly as
it does for every other command. It is the settings file that failed, not the
credential.

## Keeping the reference truthful

The reference is compiled into the binary from two sources that live only in the
development repository: the vendored contract and a hand-maintained record of the
empirical observations. Neither ships with the CLI, and neither is read at run time.

For an operator this has one consequence worth knowing: **the reference is as
current as the CLI you are running.** A contract change or a newly recorded
observation reaches you by upgrading the CLI, not by the server telling you. Run
`glassfrog --version` if you need to know how current your copy is.
